A '''square root of a 2×2 matrix''' {{mvar|M}} is another 2×2 [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] {{mvar|R}} such that {{math|1=''M'' = ''R''<sup>2</sup>}}, where {{math|''R''<sup>2</sup>}} stands for the [[matrix product]] of {{mvar|R}} with itself.  In general, there can be zero, two, four, or even an infinitude of [[Square root of a matrix|square-root matrices]]. In many cases, such a matrix {{mvar|R}} can be obtained by an explicit formula.

Square roots that are not the [[Zero matrix|all-zeros matrix]] come in pairs: if {{mvar|R}} is a square root of {{mvar|M}}, then {{math|−''R''}} is also a square root of {{mvar|M}}, since {{math|1=(−''R'')(−''R'') = (−1)(−1)(''RR'') = ''R''<sup>2</sup> = ''M''}}.

A 2×2 matrix with two distinct nonzero [[eigenvalue]]s has four square roots. A [[positive-definite matrix]] has precisely one positive-definite square root.

==A general formula==
The following is a general formula that applies to almost any 2 × 2 matrix.{{r|Bernard1}} Let the given matrix be
<math display=block>M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix},</math>
where {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|C}}, and {{mvar|D}} may be real or complex numbers.  Furthermore, let {{math|1=''τ'' = ''A'' + ''D''}} be the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of {{mvar|M}}, and {{math|1=''δ'' = ''AD'' − ''BC''}} be its [[determinant]].  Let {{mvar|s}} be such that {{math|1=''s''<sup>2</sup> = ''δ''}}, and {{mvar|t}} be such that {{math|1=''t''<sup>2</sup> = ''τ'' + ''2s''}}.  That is,
<math display=block>s = \pm\sqrt{\delta}, \qquad t = \pm\sqrt{\tau + 2s}.</math>
Then, if {{math|''t'' ≠ 0}}, a square root of {{mvar|M}} is
<math display=block>
  R = \frac{1}{t}\begin{pmatrix} A + s & B \\ C & D + s \end{pmatrix}
    = \frac{1}{t}\left(M + sI\right).
</math>

Indeed, the square of {{mvar|R}} is 
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  R^2  &= \frac{1}{t^2}\begin{pmatrix}
            A^2 + B C +  2 s A + s^2 & A B + B D + 2 s B \\
            C A + D C +  2 s C & C B + D^2 + 2 s D + s^2
          \end{pmatrix} \\[1ex]
       &= \frac{1}{t^2}\begin{pmatrix}
            A^2 + B C + 2 s A + A D - BC & A B + B D + 2 s B \\
            A C + C D + 2 s C            & B C + D^2 + 2 s D + A D - B C
          \end{pmatrix} \\[1ex]
       &= \frac{1}{A + D + 2 s}\begin{pmatrix}
            A(A + D + 2 s) & B(A + D + 2 s) \\
            C(A + D + 2 s) & D(A + D + 2 s) 
          \end{pmatrix} = M.
\end{align}</math>

Note that {{mvar|R}} may have complex entries even if {{mvar|M}} is a real matrix; this will be the case, in particular, if the determinant {{mvar|δ}} is negative.  

The general case of this formula is when {{mvar|δ}} is nonzero, and {{math|''τ''<sup>2</sup> ≠ 4''δ''}}, in which case {{mvar|s}} is nonzero, and {{mvar|t}} is nonzero for each choice of sign of {{mvar|s}}. Then the formula above will provide four distinct square roots {{mvar|R}}, one for each choice of signs for {{mvar|s}} and {{mvar|t}}.

===Special cases of the formula===
If the determinant {{mvar|δ}} is zero, but the trace {{mvar|τ}} is nonzero, the general formula above will give only two distinct solutions, corresponding to the two signs of {{mvar|t}}.  Namely,
<math display=block>
  R = \pm\frac{1}{t}\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}
    = \pm\frac{1}{t} M,
</math>
where {{mvar|t}} is any square root of the trace {{mvar|τ}}.

The formula also gives only two distinct solutions if {{mvar|δ}} is nonzero, and {{math|1=''τ''<sup>2</sup> = 4''δ''}} (the case of duplicate [[eigenvalue]]s), in which case one of the choices for {{mvar|s}} will make the denominator {{mvar|t}} be zero.  In that case, the two roots are
<math display=block>
  R = \pm\frac{1}{t}\begin{pmatrix} A + s & B \\ C & D + s \end{pmatrix}
    = \pm\frac{1}{t} \left(M + s I \right),
</math>
where {{mvar|s}} is the square root of {{mvar|δ}} that makes {{math|''τ'' − 2''s''}} nonzero, and {{mvar|t}} is any square root of {{math|''τ'' − 2''s''}}.

The formula above fails completely if {{mvar|δ}} and {{mvar|τ}} are both zero; that is, if {{math|1=''D'' = −''A''}}, and {{math|1=''A''<sup>2</sup> = −''BC''}}, so that both the trace and the determinant of the matrix are zero. In this case, if {{mvar|M}} is the null matrix (with {{math|1=''A'' = ''B'' = ''C'' = ''D'' = 0}}), then the null matrix is also a square root of {{mvar|M}}, as is any matrix
<math display=block>
R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ c & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\quad \text{and} \quad
R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & b \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
</math>
where {{mvar|b}} and {{mvar|c}} are arbitrary real or complex values. Otherwise {{mvar|M}} has no square root.

==Formulas for special matrices==

===Idempotent matrix===
If {{mvar|M}} is an [[idempotent matrix]], meaning that {{math|1=''MM'' = ''M''}}, then if it is not the identity matrix, its determinant is zero, and its trace equals its [[rank of a matrix|rank]], which (excluding the zero matrix) is {{math|1}}. Then the above formula has {{math|1=''s'' = 0}} and {{math|1=''τ'' = 1}}, giving {{mvar|M}} and {{math|−''M''}} as two square roots of {{mvar|M}}.

===Exponential matrix===
If the matrix {{mvar|M}} can be expressed as real multiple of the exponent of some matrix {{mvar|A}}, <math>M = r \exp(A)</math>, then two of its square roots are <math>\pm\sqrt{r}\exp\left(\tfrac{1}{2}A\right)</math>. In this case the square root is real.{{r|Harkin2}}

===Diagonal matrix===
If {{mvar|M}} is diagonal (that is, {{math|1=''B'' = ''C'' = 0}}), one can use the simplified formula
<math display=block>R = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & d \end{pmatrix},</math>
where <math>a = \pm\sqrt{A}</math>, and <math>d = \pm\sqrt{D}</math>. This, for the various sign choices, gives four, two, or one distinct matrices, if none of, only one of, or both {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|D}} are zero, respectively.

===Identity matrix===
Because it has duplicate [[eigenvalue]]s, the 2×2 [[identity matrix]] <math>\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)</math> has infinitely many [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] rational square roots given by 
<math display=block>
  \frac{1}{t} \begin{pmatrix}  s &  r\\  r & -s\end{pmatrix} \text{ and }
              \begin{pmatrix} \pm 1 &  0\\  0 & \pm 1\end{pmatrix},
</math>
where {{math|(''r'', ''s'', ''t'')}} are any complex numbers such that <math>r^2 + s^2 = t^2.</math>{{r|Mitchell}}

===Matrix with one off-diagonal zero===
If {{mvar|B}} is zero, but {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|D}} are not both zero, one can use
<math display=block>R = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \\ \frac{C}{a + d} & d \end{pmatrix}.</math>

This formula will provide two solutions if {{math|1=''A'' = ''D''}} or {{math|1=''A'' = 0}} or {{math|1=''D'' = 0}}, and four otherwise.  A similar formula can be used when {{mvar|C}} is zero, but {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|D}} are not both zero.
===Real matrices with real square roots===
The [[algebra over a field|algebra]] {{math|M(2, '''R''')}} of 2×2 real matrices has three types of planar [[subalgebra]]s. Each subalgebra admits the [[exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential map]]. If <math>p = \exp(q)</math>, then <math>\pm \exp\left(\tfrac{q}{2}\right)</math> are square roots of {{mvar|p}}. The condition that the matrix is the image under exp limits it to half the plane of [[dual number]]s, and to a quarter of the plane of [[split complex number]]s, but does not constrain ordinary [[complex plane]]s since the exponential mapping covers them. In the split-complex case there are two more square roots of {{mvar|p}} since each quadrant contains one.
